platforms.title: Screen Eye Strain: It's Not Blue Light, It's How You Blink
platforms.meta_description: Does the 20-20-20 rule work? It eases screen eye strain only while you keep it up, and blue-light lenses don't help. What works, plus UK eye-test rights.
platforms.body_html:
By mid-afternoon the text on your monitor starts to swim, your eyes feel gritty, and you catch yourself rubbing them between emails. The internet's favourite fix is the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet (about 6 metres) away for 20 seconds. A close second is a pair of blue-light glasses. One of these has reasonable evidence behind it, and it is not the glasses. Most screen eye strain comes from how we use our eyes at a screen, not from the light it gives off, and that changes which habits are worth your time.

Why screens tire your eyes

The first culprit is blinking. The American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) notes that people normally blink about 15 times a minute, but studies show that rate drops to about 5 to 7 times a minute while using computers and other digital devices. Each blink spreads a fresh layer of tears across the front of the eye. Blink less, and the eye surface dries out, which is why long screen days so often end with stinging, gritty or watery eyes. The NHS lists looking at computer screens for a long time without a break among the things that make dry eyes more likely, alongside air-conditioned or heated rooms and smoking.

The second culprit is distance. Holding focus at arm's length for hours keeps the eye's focusing system working without a pause. The Health and Safety Executive (HSE), the UK's workplace regulator, says long spells of display screen work can lead to tired eyes, discomfort, temporary short-sightedness and headaches. The key word is temporary: HSE states that screen work does not cause permanent damage to eyes, and the AAO says the old warnings about screens "ruining" your eyesight are not true either.

Blue light gets most of the blame, yet the best evidence does not back that up. A 2023 Cochrane systematic review by Singh and colleagues looked at 17 randomised controlled trials and concluded that blue-light filtering lenses may not reduce eye strain from computer use compared with standard lenses over the short term. For visual fatigue, follow-up was under a week and the certainty of the evidence was low. The AAO also points out that computer glasses made for screen distance are not the same thing as blue-light blocking glasses.

So what actually helps?

The 20-20-20 rule helps while you keep doing it. In a 2023 study in Contact Lens & Anterior Eye, Talens-Estarelles and colleagues installed break-reminder software based on the rule on the laptops of 29 computer users who already had symptoms. Over two weeks they took more breaks a day, and their scores for digital eye strain and dry eye symptoms went down. One week after the reminders were switched off, the improvement had not held, and objective tear-film measurements did not change during the two weeks. It was a small before-and-after study without a control group, so the honest reading is that the rule eases symptoms as an ongoing habit, not as a one-off cure.

Break little and often rather than long and rarely. HSE says there is no legal guidance on how long or how often breaks should be for screen work, but short, frequent breaks are better than longer, rarer ones: for example, 5 to 10 minutes every hour is better than 20 minutes every 2 hours. Ideally a break lets you get up and move, not just switch to your phone.

Set up the screen and the room. The AAO suggests sitting about 25 inches, roughly arm's length, from the screen, with your gaze angled slightly downward, matching screen brightness to the light around you and turning the contrast up. A matte screen filter can cut glare. The NHS adds keeping the screen just below eye level and using a humidifier if the air is dry.

Use your workplace rights. Under UK law, an employer must arrange and pay for a full eye and eyesight test, by an optometrist or doctor, for a display screen equipment user who asks for one. If the test shows you need glasses prescribed specifically for the distance you view your screen at, the employer pays for those too; if your ordinary prescription works, they do not have to.

So why do your eyes feel wrecked by 4 p.m.?

Back to the opening question. Your eyes are drying out from fewer blinks and staying locked on one distance for hours, and both ease with rest. That is why the 20-20-20 rule only works while you keep it up, and why the right prescription for screen distance can do more than a blue-light coating.

Some symptoms are not eye strain at all. The NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or contacting NHS 111 if your eye is painful and red, or if you have a red eye and wear contact lenses. Get immediate help for changes to your sight such as wavy lines, flashing or loss of vision. If gritty, tired eyes keep coming back despite regular breaks, book an eye test with an optometrist: screen work is visually demanding, and HSE notes it can make you aware of eyesight problems you had not noticed before, including age-related changes. This article is general health information and does not replace advice from a professional who has examined your eyes.

Sources: AAO, "Computers, Digital Devices, and Eye Strain"; HSE, "Working safely with display screen equipment" (eye tests; work routine and breaks); NHS, "Dry eyes" (reviewed January 2025); Singh S et al., Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2023; Talens-Estarelles C et al., Contact Lens & Anterior Eye, 2023.
